title: The body scan
hook: moving attention from feet to head, central to Jon Kabat-Zinn's MBSR course (1979), drawn from Buddhist practice

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thoreau and the art of going nowhere in particular. Your line was saunter. Where did your feet take you? Day one hundred thirty-two.

Quick question: how are your feet right now? You probably had to go and check. That's normal. Most of the day we live about six inches behind our eyes, and the rest of the body is something that carries the head around. It only gets our attention when it hurts. In 1979, in a hospital in Worcester, Massachusetts, a scientist named Jon Kabat-Zinn started a course for patients with chronic pain and illness that doctors had run out of ways to help. One of the first things he taught them was to lie down and visit their own bodies, one part at a time, starting at the toes. Today's practice is the body scan.
screen: `HOW ARE YOUR FEET?` → `A HOSPITAL, 1979.` → `THE BODY SCAN.`

segments.voice: The course was called Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, MBSR for short, begun at the University of Massachusetts Medical Center. It's eight weeks long, and the body scan sits right at the start. You lie on your back and move your attention slowly: the toes of the left foot, the sole, the heel, the ankle, up the leg, then the right, the hips, the belly, the back, the hands, the arms, the shoulders, the neck, the face, the top of the head. At each place you simply notice. Warm, cold, tingling, aching, nothing at all. Nothing at all counts too. You're not trying to relax, though that often happens. You're trying to be there. Kabat-Zinn was open about where he learned this: from Buddhist meditation, which he practiced for years before shaping it for a hospital. And the roots go deep. In the Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha's great teaching on mindfulness, one exercise is to review this very body from the soles of the feet up, and from the crown of the head down. The word in Pali is kayagatasati, mindfulness of the body. MBSR set the religious framing aside so anyone could use it, and it's been studied a great deal since, with real but moderate benefits for stress. Here's why it's worth five minutes. You spend all day living in your body. The scan is a way of showing up there on purpose, and saying, part by part: here I am.
screen: `MBSR: EIGHT WEEKS, 1979.` · `TOES TO THE TOP OF THE HEAD.` · `NOT RELAXING: BEING THERE.` · `ROOTS IN BUDDHIST PRACTICE.` · then, large: `HERE I AM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a short scan, feet to head. Sit or lie down. Start at your feet: what's there? Warmth, pressure, nothing. Move to the legs. The belly, rising and falling. The back against the chair or floor. The hands. The shoulders. The jaw. The eyes. The top of the head. Don't fix anything. Just visit. At the end, feel the whole body at once, and say inside: here I am. Later, if you can, try a slower one, five minutes. The bell holds the time.
The body scan. Attention moving slowly from the feet to the head, noticing without fixing, taught in MBSR and drawn from Buddhist practice. Today's word.
Your line: here I am. Today, once, scan feet to head for five minutes, lying down or sitting, and finish with your line. Day one hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: In Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction courses, participants practice a guided body scan, usually lying down for about forty-five minutes, moving attention slowly through the body from the feet to the head.

match.prompt: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
pairs: from the soles up, the crown down

myth: the goal of the body scan is to relax
the goal is to be there and notice; relaxing often happens, but it isn't the aim.
feeling nothing in a body part counts as noticing
warm, cold, tingling, aching, or nothing at all: all of it counts.
Kabat-Zinn invented the body scan with no outside source
he said openly that he drew it from Buddhist meditation he'd practiced for years.

fork.setup: you're scanning, and you reach your left knee. it feels like nothing at all. what do you do?
options: keep searching until you feel something.
give up; you're doing it wrong.
fork.reveal: nothing at all counts. you note it and move on. the scan is about showing up, not about finding sensations.

original.note: Pali, kayagatasati: mindfulness (sati) gone to the body (kaya). the old name for attention to the body.

trapdoor: what you thought: a relaxation trick from a wellness app.
what it means: moving attention slowly through the body, noticing without fixing.
what a scholar hears: MBSR (UMass, 1979) adapted it from Buddhist practice; the Satipatthana Sutta reviews the body from the soles up and the crown down.

sources.ref: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, University of Massachusetts Medical Center (1979)

notes: Audit 2026-09-30: practice called a five-minute scan 'the long version' while howItsDone says the MBSR scan runs about forty-five minutes; now 'a slower one'. Replaced the stock phrase 'the quiet gift of it'.
Kabat-Zinn named and paraphrased, never quoted. Confirm MBSR began in 1979 at the University of Massachusetts Medical Center (Worcester).

MN 10's body-parts contemplation reviews the body 'up from the soles of the feet and down from the crown of the head'; paraphrased. The MBSR sweep is also often traced to the U Ba Khin / Goenka vipassana lineage; the script says only 'Buddhist meditation'.
'Real but moderate benefits for stress' summarizes meta-analyses of MBSR (e.g. Khoury et al. 2015); confirm the hedge is fair.
Carry keeps the index's capital 'I' (here I am).
